SOURCE: "Tool Learning with Foundation Models", Yujia Qin, Shengding Hu, Yankai Lin, ... Zhiyuan Liu, Maosong Sun (about 40 authors; Tsinghua, Renmin, UIUC, NYU, CMU and others). The file is arXiv:2304.08354v3, dated 6 Aug 2024. The PDF does not name a journal anywhere, so I could not confirm ACM Computing Surveys from this text. Cite it as a preprint unless you check the venue somewhere else.

COVERAGE: I read about 321,653 of 321,653 extracted characters, all 75 pages. That covers the body (pp. 1–35), the contributions statement, and Appendix A case studies A.1–A.18 (pp. 50–75). The reference list (pp. 36–49) I skimmed for origins only. Table 1's text extraction runs the two model rows together, so I rendered page 23 as an image and checked every value against it.

CLAIMS
- claim: The survey's own experiment covers 18 tools, not 17. It tests text-davinci-003 and ChatGPT under three conditions: no tool, zero-shot prompting and few-shot prompting.
  number: 18 tools, 2 models, 3 settings
  setup: Zero-shot gives the task description plus API documentation. Few-shot adds worked tool-use examples. "No tool" is run only where a task can be done without a tool.
  quote: "We select 18 representative tools for evaluation and place the main results in this section." / "we choose both text-davinci-003 and ChatGPT to evaluate their performance with zero-shot prompting and few-shot prompting"
  where: p.21 §4; p.24 §4.2
- claim: On the curated test sets, a task is scored from the whole trace of API calls, not the final answer. It counts as correct only if a human judges every call accurate and the result reasonable.
  number: none
  setup: Applies to the 12 tools with curated test sets. Those queries were written by hand as seeds, expanded with ChatGPT and filtered by hand.
  quote: "for these manually curated test sets, we employ the trace of API calls as the metric for evaluating the models' performance. Specifically, if humans judge that all the API calls are accurate for the given task, and they yield a reasonable result, the task is deemed to be correctly completed."
  where: p.25 §4.2
- claim: For the 6 tools on existing benchmarks, scoring is by outcome: F1 on MLQA, accuracy on ASDiv, accuracy on RealTimeQA multiple choice, and ALFWorld success rate. Slides is scored by whether the generated calls execute without error. Database is scored by whether the right results come out. So the paper mixes outcome-based and trajectory-based scoring.
  number: e.g. MLQA 200 instances
  setup: Translator: NLLB on MLQA, 200 samples, F1. Calculator: accuracy. Slides: 100 tasks.
  quote: "We evaluate the model's performance by counting the fraction of instances in which the model-generated API calls are correctly executed without errors." / "The evaluation metric is the ratio of queries for which tool learning can accurately output the results."
  where: p.22 (Slides); p.24 (Database); p.21 (Translator)
- claim: The authors say themselves that the metrics differ across tools, so scores cannot be compared directly between tools.
  number: none
  setup: Table 1 as a whole
  quote: "it is important to acknowledge that the evaluation setups of these tools are inherently different, making direct comparison difficult."
  where: p.25
- claim: Zero-shot tool use can score below using no tool at all on tasks the model could do from its own knowledge. Few-shot tool use always beat no tool.
  number: Calculator/ASDiv for ChatGPT: 91.7 with no tool, 74.1 zero-shot, 92.5 few-shot. Wikipedia/HotpotQA for davinci: 33.5, 28.5, 35.5. Search/RealTimeQA for ChatGPT: 50.0, 43.3, 63.3.
  setup: Table 1. Top row is text-davinci-003, cyan row is ChatGPT. I confirmed which row is which from the rendered image.
  quote: "utilizing tools with zero-shot prompting could sometimes lead to worse performance, which implies that sub-optimal utilization of tools may negatively impact performance. Nevertheless, incorporating tools with few-shot prompting still consistently yields superior performance than not incorporating tools."
  where: p.25; Table 1 p.23
  - Caveat: one case contradicts "consistently". On Wikipedia/HotpotQA, ChatGPT scored 34.5 with no tool and 19.0 few-shot.
- claim: Tools whose arguments are executable code, such as SPARQL for knowledge graphs, are much harder. KGs, Wikipedia, online shopping and 3D modelling stay poor even with few-shot prompting.
  number: KGs few-shot: 46.9 (davinci), 14.1 (ChatGPT). 3D models: 40.0 for both. Online shopping: 37.1 / 35.9.
  setup: KGs uses 7 APIs and 64 curated questions. 3D uses 14 APIs and only 10 questions.
  quote: "for several tools such as KGs, Wikipedia, online shopping, and 3D model construction, the model performance is still far from satisfactory even with few-shot prompting." / "tools requiring the generation of executable code as the parameter to the API, such as the search_by_query API in the KGs tool ... are found to be significantly more arduous."
  where: p.25
- claim: Map, Weather, Slides, Tables, Cooking and AI Painting reach high completion rates with few-shot prompting.
  number: Weather 99.0/99.0; Map 86.8/86.8; Tables 85.2/92.2; Cooking 98.0/90.0; AI Painting 100.0/88.0
  setup: Curated sets; scores are judged from the API-call trace
  quote: "under the few-shot prompting setting, certain tools such as Map, Weather, Slides, Tables, Cooking Assistant, and AI Painting exhibit a satisfying completion rate."
  where: p.25
- claim: ChatGPT, which was trained with RLHF, did not beat text-davinci-003. The authors suggest an "alignment tax" or a smaller model as reasons, but this is speculation.
  number: e.g. Map zero-shot: 58.1 (davinci) vs 29.7 (ChatGPT); KGs zero-shot: 42.2 vs 7.8
  setup: Table 1
  quote: "although ChatGPT has been fine-tuned with RLHF, it does not yield better results than text-davinci-003. We attribute this to two reasons: firstly, the alignment tax issue ... secondly, the model size of ChatGPT, though not officially stated, might be much smaller"
  where: p.25
- claim: The survey splits environment feedback into result feedback (did the whole task succeed) and intermediate feedback (the state change after each action). This is the same split as outcome vs trajectory, applied to training signals.
  number: none
  setup: Conceptual (§3.3.2). WebShop's hand-coded reward is given as the example of result feedback.
  quote: "(1) result feedback, which is ultimate feedback returned from the environment, indicating whether the model's actions have successfully completed the task or not ... (2) intermediate feedback, which refers to the state change of the environment triggered by an action."
  where: pp.18–19
- claim: The survey argues that tool-use performance could serve as a "next-generation gauge" of machine intelligence. It proposes this without giving any benchmark.
  number: none
  setup: Opinion in §5.7
  quote: "We contend that the tool learning performance can serve as a next-generation gauge for measuring machine intelligence"
  where: p.33
- claim: All 18 tools ship in BMTools, an open-source repository. The code and curated datasets were promised for release.
  number: none
  setup: github.com/OpenBMB/BMTools
  quote: "we implement and integrate all the above tools into BMTools"
  where: p.24

LIMITS:
- The test sets are small. Some tools have very few examples: 3D models n=10, AI Painting n=25, RealTimeQA n=30, Cooking n=50, Database n=50. No confidence intervals, variance or repeated runs are reported.
- Trajectory scoring is human judgement of "accurate" calls. The paper reports no rubric, number of raters or agreement figure. The contributions section names only four people in "the human evaluation for some experiments" (p.35).
- The curated queries were generated by ChatGPT, which is also one of the models under test. The authors do not discuss this circularity. Their only evidence of diversity is "We find empirically that the generated examples are diverse enough."
- The text and the table disagree in places. Calculator says "ASDiv ... and MathQA", but Table 1 shows only ASDiv. Stock says "1200 question-answer pairs", but the table has test size 122. Map and Stock say accuracy or crowdsourced queries but give no clear metric.
- No numbers on failure modes. The analysis is one paragraph plus case studies. Appendix A shows only one ChatGPT case per tool, apparently picked as successes.
- The appendix traces also contain errors the authors do not comment on:
  - Online shopping (p.67): the model clicks the demonstration's item ID [B078GWRC1J] instead of the item it chose, and names B08GXD5MDG, which never appeared in the results.
  - Movie Hunter (p.58): the model's thought repeats the demo text "drama ... top 2" when the query asked for comedy, top 5.
  - Search engine (p.59): the model calls search_top3 and load_page_index, but the documented APIs are Search and LoadPage.
- Dated: the models are text-davinci-003 and the Mar 23, 2023 ChatGPT. There are no native function-calling APIs, and the conclusions about prompting predate those APIs. Auto-GPT, LangChain and ChatGPT Plugins are described as current.
- Out of scope: the survey offers no benchmark design, no cost or latency measurements, no safety evaluation, and no multi-step multi-tool benchmark. It says multi-step multi-tool work is barely explored (p.16).

BUILDS ON:
- Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023): translator and calculator setups.
- ReAct (Yao et al., 2022b): Wikipedia tool and ALFWorld setting.
- WebShop (Yao et al., 2022a).
- ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021).
- RealTimeQA (Kasai et al., 2022).
- MLQA (Lewis et al., 2020a); ASDiv (Miao et al., 2020); MathQA (Amini et al., 2019).
- HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018b).
- Self-instruct-style query generation (Wang et al., 2022b).
- WebGPT (Nakano et al., 2021).
- RLHF (Christiano et al., 2017); alignment tax (Ouyang et al., 2022).
- Augmented language models survey (Mialon et al., 2023).

CODE: Weather-API prompt pair, Fig. 4, p.13 (the 2-day loop inside the extraction lost its indentation):
```
Zero-shot Prompting: Here we provide a tool (API) "forecast_weather(city:str, N:int)", which could forecast the weather about a city on a specific date (after N days from today). ...
Question: "What's the temperature in Shanghai tomorrow?"
return forecast_weather("Shanghai", 1)["temperature"]
```
Map trace, where the call sequence itself is what gets graded (p.68):
```
ADD(DIVIDE(DISTANCE(start='Dallas', target='Houston'), 70),DIVIDE(DISTANCE(start='Houston', target='Austin'), 70))
```

FIGURES:
- Table 1, p.23 (a table, so the caption script does not list it): all 18 tools by # APIs, test set, n, and No Tool / Zero-shot / Few-shot for both models. It shows at a glance that the effect of tools is uneven, and it has the zero-shot regressions. The extracted text interleaves the two model rows, so read the rendered page, not the text.
- Fig. 5, p.15: introspective vs extrospective reasoning, i.e. a static plan vs a closed loop with the environment. This is a quick visual for why trajectories need evaluating.
- Fig. 3, p.11: controller / perceiver / tool set / environment loop.
- Figs. 8–9, pp.32–33: ChatGPT handling a conflict between tool output and its own knowledge (Real Madrid 13 vs 14 titles). These are anecdotes, not measurements.

PROBLEMS:
- Several pages (13, 28, 32–33, 64, 66, 68, 71–73) extract twice, with older draft text overlaid. The figure numbers clash: the overlaid draft numbers Figure 8 differently from the final text. I quoted from the clean final-version text.
- Table 1 interleaves the two models' rows in the extracted text. I resolved this from the rendered image (/tmp/p23.png, /tmp/p23b.png).
- Some non-Latin characters in the translation examples (A.16) are garbled.
- I found no instructions embedded in the PDF text.
